detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The six grid operators whose public interconnection queues are captured in this snapshot together show 8,381 pending requests totaling roughly 1.73 million megawatts of planned generation and storage capacity waiting to connect to the US grid as of August 30, 2026. These are projects in various stages of study and development, not built capacity, and the operators use different scope rules — MISO reports all statuses in one figure, CAISO counts only active requests, SPP tracks withdrawn requests separately, and ERCOT covers projects from study through commissioning — so the totals cannot be added into a single national picture without that caveat firmly in mind. What the data do show, operator by operator, is that MISO carries the largest single queue at 695,647 MW across 3,827 requests, followed by ERCOT at 440,018 MW across 1,797 requests, NYISO at 319,095 MW across 1,414 requests, SPP at 199,215 MW across 1,078 requests, CAISO at 71,682 MW across 265 requests, and the snapshot includes no separate PJM figure in this dataset.

For readers focused on AI data centers, the most relevant line items are storage and gas, because battery storage smooths the around-the-clock power profile that data centers require, and gas turbines are the dispatchable backup that operators lean on when renewables fall short. In ERCOT, the queue contains 160,906 MW of storage and 76,751 MW of gas alongside 151,883 MW of solar and 48,834 MW of wind, a mix that reflects the intense load growth Texas is absorbing. SPP shows 53,412 MW of storage and 47,392 MW of gas queued behind 64,737 MW of wind and 33,527 MW of solar, while CAISO's active queue is dominated by 46,944 MW of storage and only 916 MW of gas, consistent with California's policy constraints. NYISO reports 27,879 MW of gas and just 80 MW of solar in its named fuels, with the remaining 291,136 MW coded as other, a category that likely includes offshore wind and storage under NYISO's own classification conventions.

The commercial electricity sales figures, which EIA reports by state for June 2026 and which serve as a proxy rather than a direct measurement of data center load, show Texas leading at 15,754 gigawatt-hours, followed by California at 10,025 GWh, Ohio at 5,588 GWh, Georgia at 5,547 GWh, Virginia at 7,771 GWh, Illinois at 3,914 GWh, Arizona at 3,983 GWh, and Oregon at 2,216 GWh, with prices ranging from 8.66 cents per kilowatt-hour in Texas to 27.33 cents in California — cost differentials that help explain why interconnection queues in lower-price regions are swelling fastest. The number to watch in the months ahead is how many of the storage and gas projects currently in ERCOT's 160,906 MW and SPP's 53,412 MW storage queues advance from study into signed interconnection agreements, since that transition is the earliest hard signal that planned capacity is likely to reach commercial operation.
